messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The assault happened on a Tuesday evening in late October, after a long day of calls. Marcus had stopped at a convenience store near his office for a coffee, the kind of routine stop he had made hundreds of times before. A man approached him in the parking lot, smelling sharply of alcohol, and demanded his wallet. Marcus hesitated—he had worked for every dollar in that wallet, and something in him refused to hand it over without a fight. The man struck him twice, once across the jaw and once in the ribs, before grabbing the wallet and disappearing. Marcus lay on the asphalt for what felt like minutes, staring at the neon sign above the store, the smell of stale beer and cheap whiskey thick in the air around him.

In the weeks that followed, Marcus found himself replaying that moment over and over. The unwanted thoughts would arrive without warning—during a quiet moment at his desk, while he was driving between appointments, even in the middle of a conversation with a customer. He would see the man’s face, the way his eyes had widened just before the first punch. And then there was the smell. Every time Marcus caught a whiff of alcohol—a coworker’s breath after lunch, the scent drifting from a bar as he walked past—his chest would tighten and his mind would jump straight back to that parking lot. He began to avoid certain streets on his sales route, taking longer detours just to steer clear of the convenience store. He told himself it was practical, just good sense. But he also started trying hard not to think about the trauma at all, pushing the memories down whenever they surfaced, numbing his feelings with long hours of television and an extra drink before bed. It was the only way he knew to get through the day.

But the avoidance came with a cost. Marcus had always been a man who trusted his instincts, who believed he could read people and situations. Now he found himself doubting that. The event happened because of the way I acted, he would think. If I had just handed over the wallet right away, none of this would have happened. The thought circled back again and again, and with it came a deeper, more disturbing conclusion: There is something wrong with me as a person. He had never felt broken before, not like this. The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, he told his wife one night, and he meant it. He no longer knew the man who had hesitated in that parking lot, the man who now flinched at a stranger’s glance and avoided eye contact with customers who reminded him, even vaguely, of his attacker.

The negative appraisals fed the triggers in a loop he could not escape. The more he believed there was something fundamentally wrong with him, the more vigilant he became. Every unexpected smell of alcohol, every unfamiliar face near his car, every intrusive thought that slipped past his defenses—each one felt like confirmation that he was right to be afraid, that he was right to see himself as damaged. The world had become a place full of cues he could not control, and his own mind had become a source of threat he could not outrun.

What finally brought Marcus to seek help was a moment of quiet exhaustion. He had cancelled three sales meetings in one week because the route would have taken him past the store. His wife had found him sitting in the dark living room at midnight, staring at nothing, and she had asked him softly if this was how he wanted to spend the rest of his life. He did not have an answer. What he feared most was that the person he had become was permanent—that the unrecognisable man was all that was left. But he was also, for the first time, willing to find out if that was true.
